theory.heading: Start with the intended use
theory.body: A responsible material comparison begins with the intended use and the teacher-provided project requirements. A material is not suitable simply because it is familiar, inexpensive or easy to recognise. Compare the properties that matter for the task, such as condition, density, grain structure, surface quality and other approved information. Different materials may suit different purposes, so avoid deciding that one product is always best. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity.

theory.heading: Compare workability and surface
theory.body: Workability describes how a material responds to approved shaping, joining and finishing processes. It can depend on the material properties, sample condition, approved tools and process. Surface features may also matter. One product may have a smooth, even face, while another may show layers, particles, fibres or natural grain. These differences should be described as evidence rather than turned into unsupported claims. A balanced comparison explains which feature may be useful for the intended purpose and identifies any limitation or uncertainty.

theory.heading: Use cautious environmental evidence
theory.body: Resource use is another part of responsible comparison. Manufactured products may use smaller wood elements, while solid timber comes from larger sections of a tree. However, this fact alone does not prove that one option is always more sustainable. Environmental impacts can also depend on sourcing, manufacturing, adhesives, transport, durability, maintenance and waste. Use reliable information and cautious language such as may, can or depends on the context. Match the available evidence to the project requirements, and state when information is missing. If suitability or an environmental claim is unclear, pause and ask rather than guessing.

questions.question: What should guide the beginning of a responsible material comparison?
choices: The intended use and project requirements
The material nearest to the bench
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Intended use and project requirements provide the purpose for comparing materials.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Start with the intended use and focus on what should guide the comparison from the beginning.

questions.question: Which factor is relevant when comparing material suitability?
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Condition and surface quality are relevant material features that can affect suitability.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Start with the intended use and identify the properties that may matter for the task.

questions.question: Why should a student avoid saying one material is always best?
choices: Different materials may suit different purposes
Material comparisons should use appearance only
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Suitability depends on the intended use, relevant properties and project requirements.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Start with the intended use and focus on why suitability can change between purposes.

questions.question: In a suitability comparison, what does workability describe?
choices: How a material responds to approved processes
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Workability describes how a material responds during approved shaping, joining and finishing processes.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Compare workability and surface and locate the definition of workability.

questions.question: Which factors can influence workability?
choices: Material properties, condition, approved tools and process
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Workability can change with the material, its condition, the approved tools and the process.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Compare workability and surface and identify the factors that affect material response.

questions.question: Which statement is the most balanced surface comparison?
choices: The smooth sample is always better
One sample has a smooth face, while the other shows visible layers
The rougher sample is unsuitable for every task
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. This statement describes observable evidence without making an unsupported judgement.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Compare workability and surface and focus on how surface differences should be described.

questions.question: What should a balanced comparison include besides a useful feature?
choices: A claim that the product is perfect
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A balanced comparison recognises useful features as well as limitations or uncertainty.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Compare workability and surface and identify what should accompany a useful feature.

questions.question: Why does using smaller wood elements not prove that a product is always sustainable?
choices: Environmental impact depends on several parts of the product life cycle
All manufactured products have equal impacts
Sustainability depends only on surface quality
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Sourcing, manufacturing, transport, durability, maintenance and waste may all affect environmental impact.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Use cautious environmental evidence and focus on why one fact cannot prove the whole claim.

questions.question: Which wording is most appropriate when environmental evidence is limited?
choices: This material has no environmental impact
The impact may depend on sourcing and manufacturing
One product is best in every situation
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Cautious wording recognises that environmental conclusions depend on evidence and context.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Use cautious environmental evidence and identify the language recommended for uncertain claims.

questions.question: What should a student do when material suitability or environmental information is unclear?
choices: Assume the smoothest surface is best
Pause and ask rather than guessing
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Asking for clarification prevents unsupported material and environmental claims.
questions.retryFeedback: Review the final sentence of Use cautious environmental evidence and identify the response to unclear information.

written.prompt: Compare two general wood materials for an intended use by discussing one relevant property, workability, surface, resource use and one uncertainty.
written.sentenceStarter: For the intended use, material A may suit because ___. Material B may suit because ___. The available environmental evidence shows ___, but it is uncertain because ___.
written.example: For the intended use, material A may suit because it has a smooth surface. Material B may suit because its visible grain may be useful for appearance. The available evidence shows that they use wood resources differently, but their overall environmental impacts depend on sourcing, manufacturing and durability.
